messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: Thoughts on missing data for Stan
parts:
[forwarding to stan-dev]

Thanks --- that's very close to what I had in vaguely in mind
and was going to try to flesh out.

In a reasonable missing data model, we need a proper model for
the missing x, which might vary by column. One attractive feature
of this proposal is that we don't have to change the model --- the
models for the missing value can be heterogeneous (as long as the
constraints don't vary).

The one thing I was waffling back and forth on in my head was
the issue of whether to take a full vector/matrix of predictors with
NA-like placeholders or whether to have just the existing data passed
in in database form:

int n_rows;
int n_cols;
int n_observed;
int observed_row[n_observed];
int observed_column[n_observed];
real observed_value[n_observed];

There are tighter data structures for anything but the sparsest
matrices, but this seems particularly clear to me. It's just the
info you need for a "partial" matrix data structure.

Either way, we'd just need something to read in the data in R.
Of course, the models aren't exactly the same, as in JAGS/BUGS,
which is too bad, I think, but something we can live with.

- Bob

On May 8, 2014, at 11:17 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hey Bob,
>
> Just a quick follow on to the Stan discussion today since you seemed interested in thinking on design. I've had a few thoughts in the back of my brain on this for a little while so I thought I'd share in case they are in any way useful to you. Roughly speaking I was thinking of being able to write models like this;
>
> data{
> matrix[N,M] Data;
> }
>
> transformed data {
> int missing_inds[];
> missing_inds <- find_missing_values(Data);
> }
>
> parameters {
> real missing_Data[length(missing_inds)];
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> matrix[N,M] full_Data;
>
> full_Data <- fill_missing_values(Data,missing_inds,missing_Data);
> }
>
> model {
> ...
> }
>
> Here find_missing_values looks for NANs or something like that. If we didn't want to make it such a specific value, we call it something like "find_nans" so that users are clear in understanding what's going on here. Similar functions for the case where observed values are passed simply as index/value pairs would also be straight forward.
>
> Something like this would make these missing data models much easier to write and shouldn't be a lot of work to implement, assuming we fix the dump file parsing to handle nan/inf.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Thoughts on missing data for Stan
parts:
On Monday, May 12, 2014 4:55:17 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The one thing I was waffling back and forth on in my head was
the issue of whether to take a full vector/matrix of predictors with
NA-like placeholders or whether to have just the existing data passed
in in database form:

   int n_rows;
   int n_cols;
   int n_observed;
   int observed_row[n_observed];
   int observed_column[n_observed];
   real observed_value[n_observed];

There are tighter data structures for anything but the sparsest
matrices, but this seems particularly clear to me.  It's just the
info you need for a "partial" matrix data structure.

Applied statisticians rarely deal with real databases. Everything else that I know of uses the placeholder approach. Yes, you can reconstruct a matrix from that information but that is a lot of fiddling compared to the placeholder approach. Also, it is even more tedious when you have to distinguish observed to be undefined from missing (which is why we need at least two placeholder values).

On May 8, 2014, at 11:17 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

> data{
>  matrix[N,M] Data;
> }
>
> transformed data {
>   int missing_inds[];
>   missing_inds <- find_missing_values(Data);
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real missing_Data[length(missing_inds)];
> }

I would prefer a syntax like

parameters {
  full_Data(Data);
}

to imply that complete_Data is of the same type and size as Data but with the missing values replaced by proposals.

> transformed parameters{
>   matrix[N,M] full_Data;
>
>   full_Data <- fill_missing_values(Data,missing_inds,missing_Data);
> }

This would work, although I think it puts an unnecessary burden on the user relative to full_Data(Data). Also, if we have placeholders in Data, I don't see why it would be necessary to pass missing_inds.

Either way, continuous missing values can be managed but we also need ways to facilitate marginalizing out categorical missing values. To me, the easiest way to do that is to have placeholder values and change the behavior of the (non-count) PMFs to marginalize whenever they encounter a missing value. To do a logit model this databasy way, the user would have to do

data{
  int N_obs;
  int N_miss;
  int K;
  matrix[N_obs,K]  X_where_y_is_obs;
  matrix[N_miss,K] X_where_y_is_miss;
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y_obs[N_obs];
}
parameters {
  vector[K] beta;
  vector[K] psi;
}
model {
  vector[N_miss] eta_miss;
  y_obs ~ bernoulli_logit(X_where_y_is_obs * beta);
  eta_miss <- X_where_y_is_miss * beta;
  for(i in 1:N_miss) eta_miss[i] <- inv_logit(eta_miss[i]);
  increment_log_prob( eta_miss * log(eta_miss) +
                     (1 - eta_miss) * log(1 - eta_miss) );

  /* missingness model */
}

That is way more than

data {
  int N;
  int K;
  matrix[N,K] X;
  int y[N]; // has missing values
}
parameters {
  vector[K] beta;
  vector[K] psi;
}
model {
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(X * beta); // marginalizes internally
  /* missingness model */
}

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Thoughts on missing data for Stan
parts:
The one advantage of making the missing data values more explicit (and exposing the indices) is the ability to place priors on the missing data variables.  I don't work with models like this so I'm not sure how common of a use case this would be, but it seems plausible.

Automatic marginalization of discrete parameters is interesting.  It would require a large amount of work under the hood though.  In particular, representing and transferring missing values would require replacing the int type with a special "stan_int" structure which carries a present/missing flag and (probably) bounds.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Thoughts on missing data for Stan
parts:
We've had requests for marginalizing out unbounded discrete
params in Poisson-like models.

I'm hoping we can go some way to supporting R-like missing data
input without actually ripping the guts of Stan apart in terms
of data types.

I'm not talking about setting up a database per se, so much as
using data-structure-like representations. R users might be
familiar with data frames and if they're familiar with join-like
operations on those, we're there. Hadley managed to move some people
in this direction with ggplot2, but I understand it's contentious.

From Ben:

> I would prefer a syntax like
>
> parameters {
> full_Data(Data);
> }
>
> to imply that complete_Data is of the same type and size as Data but with the missing values replaced by proposals.

I hadn't thought about higher-level syntactic features like
this --- that is, something that's not either a data type or
a function. But there's no reason at all we couldn't do it
and it'd give us more flexibility.

>
> > transformed parameters{
> > matrix[N,M] full_Data;
> >
> > full_Data <- fill_missing_values(Data,missing_inds,missing_Data);
> > }

We'd probably have to do something like this, too, in transformed
parameters, but it could also be done at a higher level.

>
> This would work, although I think it puts an unnecessary burden on the user relative to full_Data(Data). Also, if we have placeholders in Data, I don't see why it would be necessary to pass missing_inds.
>
> Either way, continuous missing values can be managed but we also need ways to facilitate marginalizing out categorical missing values. To me, the easiest way to do that is to have placeholder values and change the behavior of the (non-count) PMFs to marginalize whenever they encounter a missing value.

This isn't right for all the marginalizations. If I have a mixture,
then I can't just marginalize the discrete mixture indicator, I need
to get in the rest of it. I'm not sure how to do that.

> To do a logit model this databasy way, the user would have to do
>
> data{
> int N_obs;
> int N_miss;
> int K;
> matrix[N_obs,K] X_where_y_is_obs;
> matrix[N_miss,K] X_where_y_is_miss;
> int<lower=0,upper=1> y_obs[N_obs];
> }

This still looks like the NA approach to me. What I was
thinking about is literally more database like with row and
column indices as columns --- like the dataframes you need
for ggplot2. Here that'd be more like:

data {
int<lower=0> N; // num observed
int<lower=1> I; // num rows
int<lower=1> J; // num columns
int<lower=1,upper=I> row[N]; // row for obs n
int<lower=1,upper=J> col[N]; // col for obs n
real val[N]; // value for obs n

But my point was that we could abbreviate all of this somehow
(like say the way Ben suggested declaring parameters) and let
the user just input val with missing values on the input side.

Then you need to declare the parameters to be all the other
row/column combos, and then in transformed data the combination.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Thoughts on missing data for Stan
parts:
On Wednesday, May 14, 2014 4:31:39 AM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
The one advantage of making the missing data values more explicit (and exposing the indices) is the ability to place priors on the missing data variables.  I don't work with models like this so I'm not sure how common of a use case this would be, but it seems plausible.

It should be more common than it is. But usually what could be considered a prior on a missing value is really a part of what Rubin calls the complete-data likelihood. So if you have a row vector like

2.4, NA, 7.3, 8.6, NA, NA, 1.9, ...

then it is a bit tortuous to consider 2.4, 7.3, 8.6, and 1.9 to be fixed while the NAs are unknowns to estimate. Rather you need a likelihood function for the whole vector, inclusive of NAs, and explicitly or implicitly integrate out the unknown values. For continuous unknowns, I think it is easiest to estimate them as part of the joint posterior and ignore those margins if you don't care about them. But for discrete unknowns, since Stan can't elegantly deal with them anyway, I think it is best to marginalize them out.

Automatic marginalization of discrete parameters is interesting.  It would require a large amount of work under the hood though.  In particular, representing and transferring missing values would require replacing the int type with a special "stan_int" structure which carries a present/missing flag and (probably) bounds.

Maybe. The PMFs already know the bounds for the variable as a whole, so to me the main obstacle is currently not being able to recognize NAs. Are you saying that the user should be able to specify that there is a zero probability of the unknown value taking some subset of values in the sample space for the variable? I guess to be fully Bayesian we would need to work toward that but I haven't seen a lot of papers doing that (perhaps because it would be awkward to program in whatever language).

Ben
